text: 8.3 Hello everybody. My name is Munira. I'm going to discuss something that hopefully will encourage you to think about how life will be in the very near future. I'll begin by explaining how the world's population is changing and by presenting some recent statistics. I'll then talk about what effects that will have on society and how our attitudes may need to change. It's common knowledge that people are living longer than ever before. Indeed, November 15, 2022 is otherwise known as the Day of 8 Billion, the day when the world's population reached that number for the first time in history. But here's another fact. If you look at the data I've provided here, which has been gathered by the United Nations, you'll see that it indicates that the number of people aged 65 or more has tripled in the last 40 years. It was 260 million in 1980, and it is now well over 760 million. Between now and 2050, this elderly population is likely to skyrocket from today's 10% to approximately 17%, or 1.6 billion people. To be clear, an aging population isn't something that's just happening in wealthy countries. It's happening everywhere, and it stems from improved medicine and better technology. It's also enabled by greater understanding of healthy eating and exercise habits. All this will result in a population that's getting older and older on average. Indeed, in 2020, another important point was reached. Back in the 1950s, there were far more babies than there were 65-year-olds, but this has now altered completely. Since 2020, there have been more people aged 60 or over than there are children aged 5 or under. About 8% of the population is currently aged under 5. In just a few decades' time, this will drop to around 6%. Having a large and growing elderly population can cause problems, of course, and one of the big problems has nothing to do with people getting ill or less able to do things as they get older. Many people aged 65 or older are extremely fit, smart, and as capable of working as somebody 10, 20, or even 30 years younger. There is no typical older person in the same way that there is no typical 20-year-old. The problem often comes with the way we often think about older people. Many of us tend to assume that they are weak, dependent on other people for help, or that they cannot do certain things. In many ways, this is the wrong attitude and also very unfair. We need to change our attitudes towards older people, value them more, and find better ways to include them in society. It may well be that in a decade's time, we won't even consider 65 to be old. It will just be middle-aged. Perhaps in the near future, 80 will be the new 65. Hello, my name is Lee. Thank you, Moneera, for that interesting presentation. I'm going to contribute to what Moneera has said by talking about how long people are now living compared to the past. First, I'll outline some data about life expectancy and how this is likely to change in the future. After that, I'll talk about some of the possible effects that these changes might have. So, Moneera has just explained that the overall percentage of children is much less now than it used to be, largely because of the increase in the older population. There are around 140 million babies born every day across the world. However, there has been a steady decrease in the number of births every year, as this graph shows. In the 1950s, there were five children born for every woman. The birth rate today is around 2.3. The United Nations estimates that it will drop to 2.1 by 2050. At the same time, people are living longer. Since the 1950s, the average lifespan around the world has increased from just 45 years old to 73. There are many reasons for this, and one, of course, is that improved medicine allows us to live longer. Some predict that this will increase to 86 years old by 2050. The fact that people are living longer lives will, of course, lead to huge changes in the future. Today's five-year-olds are more likely than any previous generation to live to be 100 years old. Currently, it's estimated that there are just over 600,000 centenarians, people aged 100 or over, in the world. This is projected to increase to 3.7 million by 2050, as advances in healthcare allow people to live longer. If this happens, we will have to totally rethink the way we see our lives. At the moment, most of us think of life in three phases. The first 20 years are about getting an education. The next stage involves between 30 and 45 years of work, and the final stage is retirement. But if more of us are living to become centenarians, then the idea of retiring at around 65 starts to make very little sense. Apart from economic and social problems, there are psychological ones, too. Retirement is often seen as the point when people move back from responsibilities and stop participating actively in society. For many people, it's a challenging and even worrying time. A retirement that lasts 30 years or more could be seen as a problem by many, especially among those that can't afford a comfortable lifestyle. Many things in the future will alter, and we need to ensure that we are ready for them.
